name: Ayyubid Sultanate
summary: The Sunni dynasty of Saladin, a Kurdish family that ended the Fatimid Caliphate in 1171 and ruled Egypt, Syria, the Jazira and Yemen until the Mamluks and Mongols ended it.

knownFor.label: Madrasas
knownFor.note: Sunni colleges built across Egypt and Syria.

location.value: Egypt, Syria and Upper Mesopotamia (al-Jazira), with Yemen, the Hejaz and northern Nubia at the peak.
location.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

terrain.value: The Nile valley and delta, the Syrian coast and interior, and the plains of the Jazira.
terrain.source: General geography (not checked against a source)

climate.value: Hot and dry in Egypt; wetter on the Mediterranean coast and cooler in the Syrian uplands.
climate.source: General geography (not checked against a source)

resources.value: Egypt was the economic centre; Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade passed through ports such as Aden.

disasters.value: None recorded in the sources read.
disasters.source: Not covered by the sources read for this entry

population.value: About 7.2 million in the core lands (Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, Palestine and Transjordan) in the 12th century; the total for all Ayyubid lands is unknown.

urbanisation.value: Cairo, Damascus and Aleppo were the major cities, and Italian merchants settled in Alexandria.

disease.value: None recorded in the sources read.
disease.source: Not covered by the sources read for this entry

migration.value: Kurdish groups joined the army in the 1240s and again in 1259; Italian merchants settled in Alexandria.
migration.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026)

economicBase.value: Egypt was the economic centre, and the dynasty dominated Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Red Sea and Indian Ocean routes, with Aden developed as a major port and Italian merchants at Alexandria.

wealth.value: Egypt’s revenues paid for Saladin’s large army.
wealth.source: Encyclopedia.com: Sultanates, Ayyubid (search excerpt only, page not opened)

moneyAndTax.value: Dinar and dirham coins; revenue from land was assigned to soldiers as iqta’ fiefs, on the Seljuk model.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026) (iqta’ only); Simple English Wikipedia: Ayyubid Sultanate (search excerpt, coins)

inequality.value: A ruling family and army elite held the fiefs; Christians faced some local restrictions under Saladin.

governmentType.value: A family confederation: semi-autonomous principalities held by relatives under a senior sultan.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Saladin (1174–1193), al-Adil I (1200–1218), al-Kamil (1218–1238) and as-Salih Ayyub (1240–1249).

succession.value: Disputed after each strong ruler; the senior sultan’s control depended on force or family authority, and al-Adil gave large lands to his own sons.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

institutions.value: Iqta’ fiefs on the Seljuk model; Egypt was run from Cairo while Syrian cities were largely independent.

stability.value: Family disputes returned after Saladin died (1193) and after al-Kamil died (1238); the Mamluk coup ended Ayyubid rule in Egypt in 1250.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Britannica: Ayyubid dynasty (search excerpt only, page not opened)

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the sultans’ own mamluk regiments weakened the army, and the Bahri mamluks seized Egypt in 1250.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

armyAndTech.value: Kurdish and Turkic cavalry, Arab and Fatimid contingents, and the rulers’ own mamluk units; Kurds were at most about a third of the army under Saladin.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

majorWars.value: Hattin and the recapture of Jerusalem (1187); the Fifth Crusade at Damietta (1218–21); the Seventh Crusade defeated at Mansurah (1250); the Mongol conquest of Syria (1260).

territoryChange.value: Saladin took Egypt (1169) and then Syria after 1174, Aleppo in 1183 and made Mosul a client in 1186; the Syrian lands fell to the Mongols in 1260.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were the Zengids, Crusader states, Almohads, Khwarazmians and later the Mongols and Mamluks; truces with Richard I (1192) and Frederick II (1229).

inventions.value: Military engineering: the Cairo Citadel and the defences of Aleppo.
inventions.source: Britannica: Ayyubid dynasty (search excerpt only, page not opened)

scienceEducation.value: New madrasas, including Shafi’i and Maliki colleges in Cairo, revived learning.

openness.value: A continuation of Fatimid culture; the rulers patronised poetry and manuscripts, including an Arabic translation of the Shahnameh (1224).
openness.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Britannica: Ayyubid dynasty (search excerpt only, page not opened)

communicationTransport.value: Red Sea and Indian Ocean shipping, with Aden developed as a major port.

religion.value: Sunni Islam was promoted in place of Fatimid Shi’a rule, with many new madrasas.

languageWriting.value: Arabic, Kurdish and Turkish were spoken; the region was mostly Arabic-speaking and many princes knew Arabic letters.
languageWriting.source: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026); Simple English Wikipedia: Ayyubid Sultanate (search excerpt, languages)

artsArchitecture.value: The Cairo Citadel and Aleppo’s defences; an illustrated Kalila wa-Dimna manuscript (about 1220).
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Britannica: Ayyubid dynasty (search excerpt only, page not opened)

socialStructure.value: A ruling family and army elite (Kurdish and Turkic troops, mamluks) above scholars, merchants and Christian and Jewish communities.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: Sunni Islam and loyalty to the family of Saladin; the Abbasid caliph recognised Saladin as sultan in 1174.

dailyLife.value: None recorded in the sources read.
dailyLife.source: Not covered by the sources read for this entry

neighbours.value: The Zengids, Crusader states, Almohads, Khwarazmians, the Rasulids of Yemen and later the Mongols and Mamluks.

ideasReligions.value: A Sunni revival and the madrasa model replaced Fatimid Shi’a institutions.

colonisation.value: None. Italian merchants settled in Alexandria.

riseSignals.value: Saladin took Egypt as vizier in 1169, ended the Fatimid Caliphate in 1171 and was recognised as sultan by the Abbasids in 1174.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: The late 12th century under Saladin and his early successors, with an area of about 1.7–2.0 million square kilometres.

declineSignals.value: Family disputes after 1238, divided Syrian emirs, the Mamluk coup of 1250, then the Mongol conquest of Syria in 1258–60.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

outcome.value: Egypt passed to the Bahri Mamluks in 1250 and the Syrian lands fell to the Mongols in 1260. Small branches survived at Hama (to 1341) and Hisn Kayfa; Iranica says Hisn Kayfa lasted to 1462, Wikipedia to the early 16th century.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Wikipedia and Encyclopaedia Iranica were read; Britannica blocks automated reading, so it is cited from search excerpts only.
sources.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Medium to high for dates and rulers. The start differs by source: Saladin took power in Egypt in 1169 (Iranica) and ended the Fatimids in 1171 (Wikipedia); Hisn Kayfa’s end date also differs.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Ayyubid dynasty (checked 14 Nov 2026); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ayyubids (checked 14 Nov 2026)
